newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's Telstra sale could reap A$12 bln.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's Telstra sale could reap A$12 bln.

text.p: Australian government-owned telecommunications carrier Telstra Corp could be worth as much as A$36 billion with the government reaping up to A$12 billion from its one-third sale, analysts said on Monday.

The comments came as the government prepared for its final assault in the upper house of parliament, the Senate, where it expects to secure support later on Monday for the partial privatisation of Telstra.
The government is assuming it will raise A$8.0 billion from the partial sale of Telstra.
However, Australian opposition leader Kim Beazley said on Monday the stake could be worth A$12 billion, while key Independent senator Brian Harradine believed it was worth A$15 billion.
"That's a fair comment," Austock Brokers research director David Perry said of the Labor Party leader's estimate.
"The figures I've seen around and from a source that I've talked to this morning -- a particular analyst -- were of a similar order of magnitude.
"I think about A$30 billion to A$40 billion is the impression we have of the value of the whole thing," Perry said.

ANZ Securities media analyst Bob Peters told Reuters he would be surprised if the stake sold for less than A$10 billion. "The government said A$8.0 billion almost two years ago and since that time, Telstra has reported improved profits plus market multiples have gone up a bit as well," Peters said.
"I think most people are now saying that 30 percent is probably worth closer to A$10 billion than A$8 billion."
A spokesman for Communications Minister Richard Alston said the government would not attempt to estimate the final value of the Telstra stake.
"It is definitely something the market will drive," his spokesman told Reuters.
"We would virtually have no say in it because the market decides what something is worth."
Analysts said the Telstra sale would be a huge offer no matter what its final value, although they expected the market to cope with it.

"Whether it's A$8 billion or A$10 billion or A$12 billion, it's a big number going into the market, but I still think it's a number that the market will manage," Macquarie Bank telecommunications analyst Paul Benetti said.

The key to market management of the sale was the foreign ownership limit, Perry said. Under government policy, foreigners would be limited to 35 percent of the stake with individual foreigners to be restricted to five percent.

"These things have been received very well indeed around the world so demand should be huge because of the type of issue it is and because it'll be a significant company in stock market terms," he said.
Analsyts agreed that the sale of one-third of Telstra was unlikely to take place before the final quarter of calendar 1997.
"We don't believe it will happen before at the absolute earliest the third quarter of next calendar year, but I think it's more likely to be the fourth quarter," Benetti said.

The legislation is expected to pass a final vote in the Senate with the support of the two Independents, Harradine and Mal Colston, who both declared last week their belief that the government had a mandate to sell a third of Telstra.
The government needs two extra votes to pass any legislation in the Senate, where it does not have a clear majority.
All other non-government parties are opposed to the sale.
